Docker has open-sourced docker-agent, a CLI plugin that lets developers define AI agents in a YAML file and run them with the same command grammar as containers. The repository pitches it as a way to "Build, run, and share AI agents with a declarative YAML config, rich tool ecosystem, and multi-agent orchestration," and the project is Apache-2.0 licensed.

The plugin invokes through `docker agent run` and can pull a definition straight from an OCI registry: `docker agent run myorg/agent:tag`. A third-party walkthrough at runthisai describes it as "a Docker CLI plugin by Docker Engineering that turns the Docker workflow you already know into an AI agent platform," with the agent spec being "a plain `agent.yaml` file that you can version, review, and share like any other infrastructure-as-code artifact."

Model coverage is wide. The README lists OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Mistral, xAI, and Docker Model Runner for local inference. Tool access flows through MCP — local, remote, or Docker-based servers — alongside what Docker calls "Built-in think, todo, and memory tools." Retrieval is handled with BM25, embeddings, hybrid search, and reranking.

It ships as a pre-installed plugin inside Docker Desktop 4.63+, or via Homebrew. The release train is moving fast: GitHub lists v1.149.0 as the current build. Docker's framing — "Create teams of specialized agents that delegate tasks automatically" — puts the project squarely in the crowded agent-builder space, next to the 440 agent stories and 323 open-source items we have tracked in the last 90 days.

signals.excerpt:
AutoTrust Ships NVFP4 Build of GEV-26B-Decide at 17.1 GiB VRAM | AI Weekly
...
- The NVFP4 build cuts GPU memory for weights from 51.1 GiB to 17.1 GiB, a 66% drop, by quantizing only the routed-expert projections.
- GPQA Diamond System 1 accuracy moves from 43.9% bf16 to 44.9% NVFP4, which the card calls within run-to-run noise of plus or minus 7 points over 198 questions.
- The 26B MoE hits 95% success at about 85 ms per step on a 60-task computer-use benchmark using numbered boxes plus element text.

AutoTrust AI has posted an NVFP4-quantized build of its 26B decision model that cuts GPU memory for weights from 51.1 GiB to 17.1 GiB, a 66% drop, while leaving bf16 System 1 accuracy effectively unchanged on the two benchmarks the card publishes. On GPQA Diamond the System 1 number moves from 43.9% to 44.9% across 198 questions, which the card describes as within 'run-to-run noise (198 questions: ±7 points).' HLE text multiple choice shifts from 8.4% to 9.7% over 513 questions.

The quantization is targeted. Only the routed expert MLPs — 30 layers times 128 experts, 3,840 in total — move to NVFP4, since the card notes that 'routed experts hold ~22 GB of FP4-able bf16 out of 24 B parameters' while attention, dense MLP, and routers stay in bf16. Activations use static scales calibrated on 3,072 System 1 prompts.

On a single B200 running vLLM, System 1 posts a 45 ms 'Median latency: 45 ms for single request' and 257 decisions per second with 64 concurrent clients. On a 60-task computer-use benchmark described as 'numbered boxes + element text,' the model records 95% success at roughly 85 ms per step, versus about 260 ms for JEV-27B-VL at the same success rate. The card lists FlashInfer TRT-LLM NVFP4 MoE kernels for B200/B300/GB200, CUTLASS FP4 kernels for RTX PRO 6000 and RTX 5090, and a Marlin W4A16 fallback (weights FP4, activations bf16) for H100/H200/A100.

The card is explicit about what has not been retested: 'NVFP4: compared to bf16 only on GPQA Diamond and HLE; adaptive thinking not re-evaluated.' It also notes the robot-arm pick-and-place result — 40% success on 20 scenes at 61 ms per step — trails JEV-27B-VL at 75%. The release lands in a busy stretch for open-weights inference work, which our tracker has logged 93 times in the past 90 days.

A 4-bit MoE build that preserves calibrated-probability behavior drops a 26B decision model onto a single 24 GB card, widening who can self-host agent-decision inference without renting B200-class hardware.

Tensor Machines Launches Open-Source Benchmark to Measure the True Cost of AI Compute

# Tensor Machines Launches Open-Source Benchmark to Measure the True Cost of AI Compute

 By PRNewswire On Oct 8, 2026 

#### New benchmark connects GPU performance and power consumption to the cost of useful AI output

Tensor Machines announced an open-source AI hardware benchmark designed to help data center operators answer the most pressing economic question: how much useful AI are they getting from the hardware and power they have already bought? The benchmark brings hardware behavior and workload performance into a repeatable assessment of the energy and cost required to produce useful AI output.

GPU specifications and hourly rental prices do not tell an operator how much work a system can sustain. Facility measures such as Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), describe energy overhead but do not measure the AI output produced by the equipment. Tensor Machines is developing the benchmark around output that meets a workload’s service requirements, giving operators a way to evaluate the productive capacity of their infrastructure.

“The economic value of a GPU comes from the useful work it delivers,” said Muneeb Rasool, founder and CEO of Tensor Machines. “Operators need to know what that output costs and how the answer changes with the workload, power settings and hardware condition. We are opening up the benchmark so they can measure those tradeoffs and make better use of the infrastructure they already have.”
...
Tensor’s benchmark recipe applies different loads and records how hardware draws power, heats up, sustains performance and recovers. The benchmark is designed to connect that physical response to the share of requests meeting service requirements, the energy consumed per accepted output token and the cost of that output. Repeating the same workload after a controlled change would let an operator test whether a different power setting, workload placement or cooling condition improves the result.

Tensor Machines’ proprietary physics-based models support this work by analyzing the relationships between power, heat, performance and hardware degradation. The models are in private beta with select bare-metal providers and neo-cloud design partners. The broader goal is to help operators sustain productive output and make informed decisions about hardware use and remaining productive life.

signals.excerpt:
QUASAR: Lowering the Loss Floor of Quantization-Aware Training with Loss-Aware Reconstruction · SyncAI.news
...
# QUASAR: Lowering the Loss Floor of Quantization-Aware Training with Loss-Aware Reconstruction

arXiv:2608.13966v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As large language model inference shifts toward lower precision, post-training quantization (PTQ) becomes increasingly brittle, making quantization-aware training (QAT) essential for preserving model quality. However, QAT has a structural mismatch: gradient updates are applied to latent full-precision weights, while the loss and gradients are computed on lossy reconstructions of those weights. This mismatch can lead to suboptimal training trajectories and a higher loss floor. Second-order PTQ methods address a similar problem by minimizing loss-aware reconstruction error, but applying such expensive reconstruction repeatedly during QAT as the weights evolve is impractical. We introduce QUASAR, a QAT method that brings lightweight, loss-aware reconstruction into the training loop. At each training step, QUASAR reconstructs the latent weights by searching over a small set of clipping ranges and fitting dequantization parameters through saliency-weighted least squares. We use an exponential moving average of squared gradients as the per-parameter saliency signal. Our theoretical analysis shows that optimizing QUASAR's reconstruction objective tightens both the convergence and final-loss bounds of QAT. We evaluate QUASAR across four model families and across INT4, INT3, INT2, and NVFP4 quantization formats. QUASAR consistently achieves lower training and evaluation loss than competitive QAT methods and outperforms QAT and PTQ baselines on downstream benchmarks. At INT2, QUASAR improves average accuracy over the best QAT baseline by 13.3 points with quantization-aware distillation and by 10.9 points with QAT on mathematical reasoning data. Notably, after distillation on only about 600M tokens, QUASAR's INT4 Gemma-4 E4B checkpoint outperforms the corresponding QAT checkpoint released by Google, with 66% lower KL divergence and 1.8 points higher average accuracy.

signals.title: llama.cpp's TurboQuant Compresses KV Cache to 3.25 Bits Per Value, Proving Fused Integer Attention Matters More Than Raw Bit Savings | AI Daily PhD
signals.excerpt:
A 70B parameter language model running at 500,000 tokens of context on 34 GB of VRAM, with generation throughput 79% faster than its FP16 baseline, sounds like a hardware upgrade story. It is not. The performance comes entirely from a 52 byte data structure called block_tq3, now merged into llama.cpp as native KV cache support. TurboQuant, ported from Google Research's arXiv:2504.19874, packs 128 dimensional key and value vectors into 3.25 bits per value through MSE optimal quantization with learned rotation matrices. On Llama-3 35B at 110K context, KV buffer memory drops from 768 MiB to roughly 167 MiB, a 79% reduction. On Llama-3 70B, the context ceiling on a single A100 extends from 109K tokens to over 500K. The numbers alone would make this notable. What makes it transformative is how those numbers are achieved: not through better compression alone, but through the elimination of a computational tax that prior quantization methods imposed.

The block_tq3 structure stores a 4 byte float32 scale factor and 48 bytes of packed 3 bit indices for 128 values. The quantization pipeline begins with a learned rotation matrix R drawn from SO(128), the special orthogonal group in 128 dimensions, paired with a translation vector t. Each incoming KV vector x is transformed as x' = R times (x minus t), aligning the vector into a low entropy subspace where 3 bit quantization captures more than 99.9% of variance. The 128 transformed values are split into two halves of 64, each receiving an independent asymmetric scale. Indices are clamped to the range negative four through three and packed into contiguous uint8 arrays using 128 bit SIMD instructions on both x86 and ARM. The rotation matrices themselves are computed offline via 178 iterations of Lloyd-Max optimization over real KV cache traces from Llama-3.1 8B, Llama-3.1 70B, and Gemma-2 27B. The entire training procedure fits on a single GPU in roughly two hours at a cost of approximately five dollars in cloud compute.

The pivotal engineering decision is what happens at decode time. Prior KV quantization in llama.cpp, using q4_0 and q8_0 formats, stored compressed values but dequantized them to float32 before computing attention. At short contexts this overhead is negligible. At 110K tokens, q4_0 incurred a 37% generation throughput penalty relative to FP16, dropping from 38.0 tokens per second to 24.0. TurboQuant sidesteps this entirely by fusing quantized integer arithmetic directly into the attention kernel. The dot product Q times K is computed via lookup table indexing over 3 bit codes, producing the attention logits without ever materializing full precision KV tensors. The result: 37.8 tokens per second at 110K context, statistically indistinguishable from the FP16 baseline of 38.0. On longer contexts where the memory bandwidth bottleneck intensifies, the advantage grows. Llama-3 70B at 500K tokens achieves 22.4 tokens per second versus 12.5 for FP16, a 79% speedup.
...
The research lineage runs through five years of post training quantization, beginning with SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., arXiv:2211.10438, 2022), which introduced activation outlier smoothing for INT8 inference. AWQ (Ji Lin et al., arXiv:2306.00978, 2023) refined this with per channel scaling for weights. The critical pivot to KV specific compression came with KVQuant (Yuhong Li et al., arXiv:2401.18079, 2024), the first system to apply non uniform per layer quantization to key and value caches, achieving less than 0.1 perplexity degradation at 3 bits on Llama-3. QAQ (Jiaming Tang et al., arXiv:2403.04643, 2024) advanced the theory further by proving, via Hessian analysis, that keys are less sensitive to quantization than values, motivating asymmetric bit allocation. TurboQuant synthesizes these findings into a single algorithm that uses rotation to handle outliers, per half scaling to manage asymmetry, and integer compute to eliminate the dequantization tax that every prior method accepted as inevitable.
...
Most coverage of KV cache quantization will focus on the compression ratio. A 4.6 times reduction in memory, enabling 500K context on 34 GB of VRAM, is the obvious headline. But the deeper story is that compression ratio and inference speed have been decoupled in prior approaches and recoupled in TurboQuant. Before this work, moving from FP16 to q4_0 saved 72% of KV memory but cost 37% of generation speed at long contexts. The memory savings enabled fitting longer sequences, but the speed penalty partially negated the practical benefit. TurboQuant achieves nearly identical memory savings, 79% versus 72%, while simultaneously accelerating decode by up to 79% relative to FP16. This is not a tradeoff; it is a Pareto improvement. The reason is architectural: by designing the quantization format around the compute kernel rather than bolting compression onto an existing pipeline, the format itself becomes the fast path.
...

The offline Lloyd-Max procedure is cheap enough, two GPU hours, to be applied routinely during model development. Expect quantization aware pretraining to incorporate rotation objectives within 12 months, yielding models that are natively compressible to 2 bits without post hoc optimization. The theoretical foundation, that attention error decomposes as the sum of key error and value error norms,
...
For practitioners building production systems, the actionable takeaway is immediate: switch long context deployments from q4_0 or q8_0 KV to TQ3_0 today. The llama.cpp integration is a single flag, kv-quant turboquant-3bit, compatible with any GGUF model. No separate rotation matrix files are needed; the Lloyd-Max centroids and lookup tables are baked into the binary. Profile decode throughput, not prompt throughput, as the primary metric at contexts above 32K tokens. On a 24 GB consumer GPU, Llama-3 70B Q4_K_M with TQ3_0 KV runs 256K context stable. On the same hardware with FP16 KV, the ceiling is roughly 30K tokens. For agentic workflows requiring full conversation history, this is the difference between truncation and memory.

The implications for hardware strategy are equally sharp. TurboQuant's integer compute path means that future inference accelerators optimized for low bit integer arithmetic, rather than floating point tensor cores, become first class citizens for LLM serving. AMD's CDNA3 with its INT4 matrix units, Intel's AMX with INT8 tiles, and Qualcomm's Hexagon DSP all gain relevance as inference targets. NVIDIA's moat, built on FP16 tensor core throughput, erodes when the dominant operation is a 3 bit integer lookup table indexed dot product. The ggml abstraction layer already maps these operations to platform specific SIMD, meaning that a single upstream change benefits every hardware backend simultaneously. By mid 2027, expect production inference cost per token to be determined more by memory bandwidth per dollar than by peak FLOPS.
...
The broader trajectory is now clear. KV cache management, not parameter count, is the binding constraint on practical LLM deployment. TurboQuant demonstrates that this constraint yields to algorithmic innovation at the intersection of signal processing, quantization theory, and systems engineering. The field spent 2023 and 2024 racing to scale models larger. The systems that will define 2026 and 2027 are racing to make existing models fit where they previously could not, run faster than they previously did, and cost less than they previously charged. A 52 byte block structure, a rotation matrix from 1982 era signal processing, and 178 iterations of Lloyd-Max optimization have done more for practical long context inference than the last doubling of GPU memory. That is the kind of result that reshapes roadmaps.

A single flag change in llama.cpp now compresses the key-value cache of a 35-billion-parameter language model from 64 KB per token to roughly 14 KB, a 4.6x reduction, while producing outputs byte-identical to FP16 at temperature zero. The implementation, contributed to llama.cpp's GitHub discussion #20969 by ggml-org developer kth8, ports Algorithm 1 from Google Research's TurboQuant paper (arXiv:2504.19874), accepted at ICLR 2026. At 110K context length on an RTX 4090 class GPU, the prior standard approach, q4_0 quantization, imposed a 37% decode throughput penalty relative to FP16 despite saving 552 MiB of KV memory. TurboQuant's tq3_0 format saves even more memory while recovering full FP16 decode speed, achieving roughly 1.0x to 1.1x relative throughput. The trick is not merely using fewer bits; it is never materializing FP16 intermediates at all.

TurboQuant exploits three statistical properties of post-projection KV activations that hold reliably in models with grouped-query attention (GQA) and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE): low variance norms across heads, natural sparsity in value channels, and predictable distributional shape after rotation. The quantization procedure, termed TurboQuant_mse, begins with per-channel normalization. For each D-dimensional KV vector, the method computes channel-wise mean mu_c and standard deviation sigma_c, then clips outliers beyond 3 sigma, a threshold tuned to keep relative MSE below 1%. The clipped, normalized values are then mapped to the nearest entry in a 256-entry codebook learned offline via k-means clustering over calibration activations. Despite the codebook being 8-bit in index space, aggressive bit-packing compresses the stored representation to an effective 2.8 bits per element in the tq3_0 format, packing 10 three-bit quanta into each 32-bit register with 2 bits of padding.

signals.excerpt:

 models/Qwen October 6, 2026 1 min read Auto-generated from ModelScope 

Qwen has updated the ModelScope model card for Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507-FP8, adding the FP8 quantised version of its large instruction-tuned model. The release targets hardware with native FP8 support, making it possible to serve a 235B-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 22B active parameters more efficiently. The update keeps the model's instruction-following and reasoning capabilities intact while reducing the precision of weights and activations to eight bits.

For developers, this matters because FP8 inference can cut memory use and increase throughput on supported GPUs, such as NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell generations. That translates into lower serving costs, faster response times, and easier deployment in production environments where GPU memory and bandwidth are limiting factors. It also means teams can experiment with a frontier-scale Qwen model without needing the full BF16 footprint, provided their hardware supports FP8.

The model itself is built for demanding tasks: complex reasoning, coding, long-form instruction following, and multilingual conversation. As with any quantised release, there are trade-offs. FP8 requires compatible hardware, and while quality is generally strong, it may not perfectly match higher-precision versions in every edge case.
